Person
PUR-sun
n. (an individual human being; in theology, a subsistence in the divine essence; rendering Hebrew panim in idiom, Greek prosopon, hypostasis)
From Latin persona, originally an actor's mask, then a role, then a legal party. Christian theology took the word and made it carry more than it had ever carried: not a mask over a nature but a genuine subsistence in one.

Biblical Definition

Person does two jobs in Scripture. In the ethical texts it appears in the idiom of respect of persons — the Hebrew is literally lifting up the face — and it names the sin of judging by the standing rather than the case: “thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour” (Leviticus 19:15). The prohibition cuts both ways, against flattering the powerful and against sentimental favour to the weak, because the standard is the case itself. Moses grounds it in God's own character — He “regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward” (Deuteronomy 10:17) — and Peter, standing in a Gentile house, draws the conclusion the church needed: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10:34). James makes it a sin without qualification: “if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin” (James 2:9), in a chapter about seating a rich man well and a poor man badly. The word's second job is theological, and Hebrews supplies the term: the Son is “the express image of his person” (Hebrews 1:3), Greek hypostasis — the word the church would use to confess one essence in three Persons, and two natures in one Person.

Webster 1828 Definition

An individual human being — and in Scripture's idiom, the standing that judges must ignore. God is no respecter of persons and neither may His people be. In theology the word carries the Trinity: one essence, three Persons.

expand to see more

PERSON, n. per'sn. [L. persona; said to be from sono, to sound.] An individual human being; a man, woman or child.

2. A man, woman or child, considered as opposed to things, or distinct from them.

3. In theology, one of the three subsistences in the Godhead; as the three persons in the Trinity.

4. In law, an artificial person is a corporation or body politic.

5. Respect of persons, partiality; the favoring of one to the prejudice of another. God is no respecter of persons. Acts 10.

Key Scripture

Acts 10:34 — "Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:"

Leviticus 19:15 — "Ye shall do no unrighteousness in judgment: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty: but in righteousness shalt thou judge thy neighbour."

James 2:9 — "But if ye have respect to persons, ye commit sin, and are convinced of the law as transgressors."

Deuteronomy 10:17 — "For the LORD your God is God of gods, and Lord of lords, a great God, a mighty, and a terrible, which regardeth not persons, nor taketh reward:"

Modern Corruption

“God is no respecter of persons” is quoted to mean that God treats all men identically in salvation — a universalism the phrase does not contain — while Leviticus 19:15's warning against favouring the poor is quietly dropped from the modern conscience.

expand to see more

The phrase means that God does not judge by external standing — nation, rank, wealth, or appearance. It does not mean that God treats all men identically, which would contradict the whole of Scripture: He chose Abraham and not his neighbours, Israel and not Egypt, Jacob and not Esau, and Paul devotes Romans 9 to the objection this raises and answers it with the potter and the clay rather than by denying the premise. Peter's own use fixes the sense — in every nation he that feareth God and worketh righteousness is accepted (Acts 10:35), which is a statement about the abolition of ethnic barriers, spoken as the gospel goes to Cornelius. Election is not respect of persons in the biblical sense precisely because it is not grounded in anything in the person; it is unconditional, which is the opposite of favouritism by rank.

Leviticus 19:15 contains a clause the modern conscience finds counter-intuitive: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor. Scripture's concern for the poor is relentless — the same chapter commands leaving gleanings and forbids oppressing a hired servant — and precisely for that reason it forbids bending a judgment in the poor man's favour. Justice that can be tilted by sympathy can be tilted by anything, and the poor are the first to suffer when courts decide by category rather than by case. Any framework that assigns credibility or guilt by group membership — whichever group is currently favoured — is respect of persons under a new name, and James calls it sin without qualification.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew idiom nasa panim (to lift up the face, hence to show partiality); Greek prosopolempsia (respect of persons, a New Testament coinage from the same idiom) and hypostasis (substance, subsistence, person).

expand to see more

Hebrew panim (H6440) — face, presence; in the idiom nasa panim, to lift the face, that is, to show partiality.

Greek prosopon (G4383) — face, countenance, person; the literal rendering of the Hebrew idiom.

Greek prosopolemptes (G4381) — a respecter of persons; the coinage in Acts 10:34, formed on the Hebrew idiom.

Greek hypostasis (G5287) — substance, subsistence; the word in Hebrews 1:3 rendered person, and the technical Trinitarian term.

Greek ousia — essence, being; the companion term of the Nicene settlement, one ousia in three hypostaseis.

Usage

"“God is no respecter of persons” — no judgment by rank or nation; not a statement that God treats all men identically."

"“Thou shalt not respect the person of the poor” — the clause the modern conscience skips."

"“The express image of his person” — hypostasis, the word the church took up for the Trinity."
